hook.line: The number of legal positions on a 19×19 board — far beyond the atoms in the universe. In 2016 an AI finally beat a top professional.
hook.say: Welcome to the long, long history of Go.

ch.t: A board made by a legendary king
ch.say: It crossed the sea from China to Japan.
p: A Chinese legend says the sage-king Yao made it for his son, and it appears in texts before the Common Era such as the Zuo Zhuan.
It reached Japan through Korea, and Nara’s Shōsōin still keeps a splendid 8th-century board.
st: From 17 to 19 lines; flourishes in the Tang
Said to be played in Baekje and beyond
Arrives; boards and stones survive in the Shōsōin
Go houses and castle games raise the level
Spreads worldwide; AI beats a top pro in 2016

ch.say: People have played for over 2,000 years.
tl: Appears as “yi” in texts such as the Zuo Zhuan
A stone 17×17 board is excavated; later 19×19 becomes standard
Reaches Japan; a marquetry board is kept in the Shōsōin
The shogunate supports the Honinbo and other Go houses

ch.say: You compete for the area you enclose.
ch.cap: A 19×19 board. The dots are “star points”
p: Black and White take turns placing stones; whoever surrounds more territory wins.
Surrounded stones are captured. Few rules — yet an astronomical number of positions.

cards: An old Korean form with preset stones
You can’t see your opponent’s stones

items: Go Seigen and Kitani Minoru revolutionise openings
Learns without human games and surpasses its predecessor

ch.say: Tap a card to flip it!
cards: Several Japanese idioms — like “dame” (useless) and “fuseki” (groundwork) — come from Go
What’s special about the Shōsōin board?
A treasure over 1,200 years old, inlaid with wood and ivory
What are white stones made of?
The finest are clam shell; for black, Nachi slate is famous
A rule that stops endless recapture
Points given to White for moving second
Standard corner sequences — now an everyday word
Said to come from a greengrocer who threw go games

p: A small universe spreads across the board. Where will you play first?
